title: The Lilliputians Take a Giant
content_zh:
And all around me, walking upon my body as though I were a landscape, were tiny men — no taller than my finger. Lilliputians. The first among them wore a golden helmet and carried a needle-like sword.
"Hekinah degul!" cried the foremost, pointing his weapon at my nose. I knew not what he said, but the meaning was clear enough: submit or be attacked.
I raised my hand as best I could — the cords had some give — and gestured to my mouth, hoping to communicate hunger. To my astonishment, the little men understood. They brought me tiny loaves of bread, no larger than musket balls, and barrels of wine the size of acorn cups.
I learned later that the emperor himself had ordered that I be fed. A thousand bakers and a hundred butchers had been mobilized for the effort. The logistics of feeding a giant had never before been attempted in the history of that diminutive empire.
For three days, I lay bound on the beach while the Lilliputians debated my fate in their capital. The grand council was divided. Some argued I should be executed as a threat. Others saw in me a weapon.
At last, the emperor made his decision. I would be brought to the capital — not as a prisoner, but as a guest. An engineer named Reldresal designed a great carriage, drawn by fifteen hundred of the emperor's finest horses.
As I was transported down the great road toward Mildendo, the capital city, every Lilliputian from a hundred leagues around lined the route to see the Man-Mountain. Children pointed. Old women wept. Soldiers saluted. I had become a national spectacle.
